samasa.alt: Also possible as a karmadhāraya, जगत् एव मूर्तिः ‘the world-form’, predicated of her; the bahuvrīhi suits a feminine subject described by a compound.

morph.note: Past participle of √तन्: the root-final nasal is dropped before -ta (तन् + त → तत). ‘Stretched out, pervaded’.

mantras.anvaya: सा नित्या एव, जगन्मूर्तिः; तया इदं सर्वं ततम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two nominal sentences: a description of her (नित्या एव … जगन्मूर्तिः) and a passive statement with a participle as predicate (तया … ततम्).
mantras.lit: She is eternal indeed, having the world as her form; by her all this is pervaded.
mantras.tr: She is eternal; the world is her very form, and by her all this is pervaded.

comm.t: The sage’s first answer corrects the king’s first question (‘how did she arise?’, 1.61): she is eternal and has no birth. The world is her form, and all of it is filled by her.

The phrase तया सर्वमिदं ततम् echoes the Bhagavad Gītā’s language for the pervading Absolute (येन सर्वमिदं ततम्, 2.17; मया ततमिदं सर्वम्, 9.4). The Devī Māhātmya applies to the Goddess what the Gītā says of the imperishable and of Kṛṣṇa.

samasa.alt: The pronoun stem तद् serves for every gender inside a compound; here it stands for the feminine तस्याः.

samasa.type: caturthī tatpuruṣa (with अर्थ, always compounded; used adverbially in the accusative)
samasa.sense: to bring about what the gods need done
samasa.alt: The first member कार्यसिद्धि is a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, कार्यस्य सिद्धिः; देवानाम् outside the compound depends on कार्य inside it.

morph.note: Passive imperative: श्रू-य-ताम् (the root vowel lengthened before the passive -ya). The courteous Sanskrit way of saying ‘listen’: ‘let (it) be heard (from me)’.
आविस् ‘openly, visibly’ is a gati that combines with √भू and √कृ: आविर्भवति ‘becomes visible, appears’. It describes manifestation, not birth — the key to the sage’s answer.

mantras.anvaya: तथा अपि मम (मत्तः) तत्समुत्पत्तिः बहुधा श्रूयताम्। यदा सा देवानां कार्यसिद्ध्यर्थम् आविर्भवति, (तदा …)
mantras.anvaya_en: A passive imperative sentence, then a यदा clause whose main clause (तदा …) is in 1.66.
mantras.lit: Even so, let her arising, in many ways, be heard from me. When she becomes manifest for the accomplishment of the purpose of the gods —
mantras.tr: Even so, hear from me how she comes forth, again and again. When she becomes manifest to accomplish the purpose of the gods,

comm.t: Although she is eternal, she has many ‘arisings’, and the sage will tell them. Each is a manifestation (आविर्भाव) for the gods’ need — the pattern of all three caritas.

The three caritas — the slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, of Mahiṣa, and of Śumbha and Niśumbha — are traditionally read as three such manifestations. The Gita Press pāṭha assigns them the presiding forms Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī and Mahāsarasvatī; that assignment is liturgical tradition, not stated in this verse.

sandhi.note: ā + a → ā; then the i of अपि becomes y before the a of अभिधीयते.
Visarga after u before the voiced j appears as r; the i of जगति becomes y before e.
Final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra.

samasa.vigraha: अनेकार्णवम् एकार्णवं कृतम् इति एकार्णवीकृतम्, तस्मिन्
samasa.type: gati tatpuruṣa with a cvi formation (a thing made into what it was not: the final a of एकार्णव becomes ī)
samasa.sense: when the whole world was flooded into a single sea at the dissolution
samasa.alt: The inner member एकार्णव is a karmadhāraya, एकः च असौ अर्णवः च ‘one ocean’, with savarṇa-dīrgha (एक + अर्णव).

morph.note: cvi construction: a noun + ī + a form of √कृ/√भू means ‘make (become) what was not before’ — एकार्णवी-कृत ‘made one ocean’. In the locative with जगति it is a locative absolute: ‘when the world had been made one ocean’.
Passive of अभि + √धा: the root vowel becomes ī before the passive -ya (धी-य-ते). ‘Is named’.

mantras.anvaya: (यदा सा … आविर्भवति,) तदा सा नित्या अपि लोके उत्पन्ना इति अभिधीयते। (कल्पान्ते) जगति एकार्णवीकृते यदा विष्णुः योगनिद्राम् (अभजत्), …
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is the main clause answering यदा in 1.65 (तदा … अभिधीयते). The second line opens a new यदा clause whose verb अभजत् and main clause (तदा …) are in 1.67.
mantras.lit: — then in the world she, though eternal, is called ‘born’. When Viṣṇu, the world having been made one ocean, (resorted to) Yoganidrā —
mantras.tr: then, though eternal, she is said in the world to be ‘born’. At the end of an age, when the world had become a single ocean and Viṣṇu entered his yogic sleep,
mantras.tr_note: ‘At the end of an age’ is drawn from कल्पान्ते in 1.67, and ‘entered’ renders अभजत् there.

comm.t: The answer to ‘how did she arise?’ is completed: her ‘birth’ is a way of speaking about her appearing. The second line begins the first story, set at the dissolution, when the world is one ocean and Viṣṇu lies in yogic sleep.

The distinction between eternal being and occasional manifestation governs the whole text: the Goddess of the three caritas is not three goddesses but one, appearing as the need arises. The idea runs parallel to Bhagavad Gītā 4.6–8 (अजोऽपि सन्नव्ययात्मा …), where the Lord, though unborn, comes into being from age to age for the protection of the good.

samasa.sense: at the dissolution, when one day of Brahmā closes
the two asuras of the first carita

morph.note: Absolutive of आ + √स्तॄ: the root ṝ becomes īr before -ya (स्तॄ → स्तीर्). ‘Having spread out Śeṣa’ — the serpent as Viṣṇu’s couch.
Imperfect of √भज्: augment a- + bhaja- + t. Its object योगनिद्राम् stands in the previous verse: ‘he took to yogic sleep’.
The numeral द्वि is declined only in the dual: m. nom. द्वौ.

mantras.anvaya: (यदा) भगवान् प्रभुः विष्णुः कल्पान्ते (जगति एकार्णवीकृते) शेषम् आस्तीर्य योगनिद्राम् अभजत्, तदा घोरौ विख्यातौ मधुकैटभौ द्वौ असुरौ (विष्णुकर्णमलोद्भूतौ ब्रह्माणं हन्तुम् उद्यतौ)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line ends the यदा clause begun in 1.66; the second begins the main clause (तदा …), whose predicate उद्यतौ is in 1.68.
mantras.lit: — having spread out Śeṣa, the Blessed Lord resorted (to it) at the end of the kalpa; then two terrible asuras, the renowned Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
mantras.tr: spreading out the serpent Śeṣa as his couch — then two dreadful asuras, the notorious Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
mantras.tr_note: The readable version keeps the verse’s order across 1.66–68; ‘the Blessed Lord’ and ‘at the end of the kalpa’ are rendered in 1.66’s readable line.

comm.t: The scene is set: at the dissolution, Viṣṇu lies on the serpent Śeṣa in yogic sleep on the single ocean. Two asuras, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, appear.

Śeṣa (‘the remainder’) is the serpent who remains when all else is dissolved. The first carita is traditionally presided over by Mahākālī in the Gita Press pāṭha; that is liturgical tradition, not stated in the text.

samasa.sense: born of the wax in the sleeping Viṣṇu’s ears

samasa.literal: on the lotus of the navel
samasa.sense: on the lotus that grows from Viṣṇu’s navel
samasa.alt: Or saptamī tatpuruṣa, नाभौ कमलम् ‘the lotus at the navel’; the sense is the same. विष्णोः outside the compound depends on its first member.

samasa.sense: the creator, lord of all creatures

morph.note: Past participle of उद् + √यम्: the nasal is dropped before -ta (यम् + त → यत). Used as a finite verb: ‘the two were ready (to kill)’, with the infinitive हन्तुम्.
Accusative of the masculine n-stem ब्रह्मन् (the god Brahmā): strong stem ब्रह्माण्-. The neuter ब्रह्मन् (Brahman) is a different word.

mantras.anvaya: (तौ असुरौ) विष्णुकर्णमलोद्भूतौ ब्रह्माणं हन्तुम् उद्यतौ। विष्णोः नाभिकमले स्थितः सः प्रजापतिः ब्रह्मा (तौ असुरौ … दृष्ट्वा … तुष्टाव)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the main clause of 1.67. The second introduces the subject (सः … ब्रह्मा प्रजापतिः) of a sentence whose verb, तुष्टाव, is in 1.69.
mantras.lit: — sprung from the wax of Viṣṇu’s ears, were intent on killing Brahmā. He, Brahmā, the lord of creatures, stationed on the navel-lotus of Viṣṇu,
mantras.tr: born from the wax of Viṣṇu’s ears, rose up to kill Brahmā. Brahmā, lord of creatures, seated on the lotus springing from Viṣṇu’s navel,

comm.t: The asuras are born from the sleeping Viṣṇu’s own ear-wax and set out to kill Brahmā, who sits on the lotus from Viṣṇu’s navel. The creator is threatened by what comes from the sustainer while the sustainer sleeps.
The tradition reads the image closely: danger arises from Viṣṇu himself while he is held by Yoganidrā, and Brahmā cannot wake him directly. He must turn to the power that holds Viṣṇu — the Goddess.
A modern reading: what threatens creation is born of the sleeper’s own neglect. The remedy the story offers is not force but praise — attention turned to the power at work.
